title: Score a tile in one pass on a manual tile cutter, then snap it with the breaker
instruction: Cut the tile in half on the tile cutter.
context: Tile and stone setters (O*NET 47-2044.00) cut ceramic tile on a manual rail cutter many times a day. Cutter makers and trade courses teach one steady pass of the scoring wheel from edge to edge, then a snap with the breaker over the end of the line. Running the wheel back over the score chips the glaze along the cut and lets the wheel ride out of its first track, so the break wanders, and pressing the breaker on a tile that is not scored all the way cracks it wherever it is weakest; either way the tile is wasted, and these are the two mistakes beginners make most. After the snap the handle is let go, so its spring lifts the foot off the cut halves.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A manual tile cutter is fixed to the table in front of the robot: an aluminum base plate 30 x 22 x 1.6 cm centered at x 30, y 0, with black foam pads either side of a steel breaking ridge along y 0, and a red side fence with a printed scale along y -8.2. A blue glazed ceramic wall tile, 15.2 x 15.2 x 0.8 cm, lies on the pads from x 22.5 to 37.7, its right edge against the fence, so the cut line (y 0) runs down its middle; its glaze is 2.8 cm above the table. Two steel rails, 1.2 cm across, run along x at y 2.5 and y -2.5, 5.8 cm up, between aluminum posts at x 15.2 to 17.0 and 43.5 to 45.3. On them rides a red carriage (3.4 x 8 x 2.2 cm, 200 g) with a 22 mm carbide scoring wheel under it, touching the glaze line; it starts at the near end with the wheel at x 21 (1.5 cm short of the tile) and stops at x 39.2 (1.5 cm past the far edge). A black push knob, 2.5 x 2.5 x 5 cm, sticks up from the carriage's right side at y -6.6. The red breaker handle is hinged on a pin at x 42.4, y 0, 9 cm up; it reaches 9 cm toward the robot to a black rubber grip (2.6 cm across, y 5.5 to 10) on a crossbar, and its rubber-shod breaker foot hangs from it at x 34.9, astride the cut line, 2.8 cm inside the tile's far edge. A return spring holds the handle up at 31.5 degrees, foot 4.8 cm above the glaze; pressed down to level, the foot bears on the glaze. The camera sees the tile's state: as the wheel rolls over each of six 2.5 cm lengths of the line, a near-black score line 4 mm wide appears on the glaze along y 0, and once the tile snaps it shows as two halves with a dark 6 mm gap between them along the line.
scoring: Scored at the end from the carriage's and handle's recorded motion. The score line is the wheel's travel over the tile, tracked in 1 mm cells. A stroke is the carriage moving one way; rolling back more than 3 mm in total over the stroke (more than a hand's play at a pause, added up so sawing back and forth can't hide under it) starts a new stroke. A second pass: any stroke runs the wheel over line an earlier stroke scored. The snap: the handle pressed down until the foot bears on the glaze. 0 for a second pass at any time, for a snap before one stroke has scored the whole line edge to edge (or with the carriage off its far stop), for no full pass, and while a gripper's tool point is within 4 cm of the grip or the push knob at the end. 0.25: one clean pass edge to edge, the carriage at rest at its far stop, no snap. 1.0: the clean pass, then the snap, the handle let go and back up within 5 degrees of its stop, and both arms back home and still (each tool point within 3 cm of where it started) for 1 s; the same with the arms elsewhere scores 0.9. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.9 and 1.0. In a real trial, mark both tile edges on the rail, review the video for any roll-back of the carriage over the tile and for the order of pass and snap, and check the break runs along a single clean score.
reset_notes: Lift out the cut halves, slide the carriage back to its near stop with the bed empty (so the wheel never crosses the new tile), lay a fresh tile against the fence on the outline, and let the handle rise to its stop.
fidelity: The cutter is a modeled articulation at about 0.6 scale (the tile full size): a carriage on a slide with drag and a handle on a hinge with a return spring. Nothing is cut or broken: the score line is the wheel's recorded travel, drawn 4 mm wide (a real score is a hairline), the wheel's pressure is assumed, and the snap is the foot reaching the glaze; the split halves are then drawn, the tile staying one fixed piece. The handle is hinged at the far stop, not on the carriage.
